title: Spin-Polarized Magnetic Metal Electrodes for Magnetic Tunnel Junctions
authors: Zhiyuan Duan, Peixin Qin, Li Liu, Guojian Zhao, Sixu Jiang, Xiaoyang Tan, Jingyu Li, Xiaoning Wang, Ziang Meng, Zhiqi Liu
abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions are foundational components of spintronic memory, sensing, and computing, and their performance depends critically on the magnetic metallic electrodes. This Perspective examines electrode materials through the lens of magnetic order and the distinct microscopic mechanisms that generate spin-selective tunneling. Conventional ferromagnets, including CoFeB and half-metallic Heusler alloys, support exchange-split electronic states and symmetry-filtered tunneling, whereas compensated collinear and noncollinear antiferromagnets exploit sublattice selectivity, spin-orbit anisotropy, vector spin textures, and magnetic multipoles. Altermagnets provide a collinear, zero-net-moment route based on symmetry-allowed momentum-dependent spin splitting. Across these material classes, we compare the origins of tunneling polarization, the roles of barrier evanescent states and interface termination, and strategies for electrically writing and reading the relevant magnetic order. This comparison reveals a broader design principle: effective electrode polarization is not a scalar bulk quantity, but a momentum-, orbital-, symmetry-, and interface-resolved transport property. Beyond the pursuit of ever larger tunneling magnetoresistance, future progress will depend on converting the unconventional spin polarization of emerging magnetic metals into electrically addressable, thermally robust, and reproducible tunneling functionality at realistic interfaces.
summary: This perspective review examines the physics governing spin-selective tunneling in MTJs, arguing that polarization is not a bulk property but a complex, symmetry-dependent transport feature. It compares traditional ferromagnets with advanced materials like antiferromagnets and altermagnets. The work concludes that future spintronic progress requires engineering these unconventional spin polarizations into robust, addressable functionalities.
main_problem: The paper aims to advance the understanding of spin-selective tunneling in Magnetic Tunnel Junctions (MTJs) beyond simply maximizing the Tunneling Magnetoresistance (TMR). It seeks to establish a comprehensive design principle for electrode polarization.
main_result: Effective electrode polarization is not a simple scalar bulk quantity but rather a complex transport property resolved by momentum, orbital symmetry, and the specific interface structure.
method: The analysis involves comparing theoretical models (Jullière vs. symmetry-filtered tunneling) with experimental observations across various magnetic material classes.
model_or_system: The core system is the Magnetic Tunnel Junction (MTJ), comprising two magnetic electrodes separated by a tunneling barrier. The discussion spans conventional ferromagnets, half-metals, antiferromagnets (AFMs), and altermagnets.
key_observables: Tunneling Magnetoresistance (TMR), effective transport polarization ($P_T$), and the degree of spin-splitting in electronic states.
important_parameters: Momentum ($\mathbf{k}_{||}$), orbital symmetry, interface termination, and magnetic order (collinear vs. noncollinear).
main_assumptions: The analysis builds upon the limitations of the simple Jullière model and highlights the necessity of considering quantum mechanical tunneling matrix elements.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes reference comparisons between TMR in amorphous vs. crystalline barriers, and the role of specific electronic states ($\Delta_1$ state in MgO).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by reviewing the historical development of MTJ physics, contrasting simple bulk polarization models with advanced quantum-mechanical descriptions, and finally surveying emerging materials like AFMs and altermagnets for future device design.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the emphasis on symmetry filtering and momentum-resolved transport properties echoes concepts used in understanding quantum transport in mesoscopic systems, which is relevant to open quantum systems.
